This page is docs/DEVELOPERS.md in the repository. The repository copy is the source; this is the same text with its links rewritten for the wiki.

Working on VeilVoice: the shape of the repository

This is the developer's way in. It is not the user guide (docs/USER_GUIDE.md) and not the reference (a page for every crate and every file, in the wiki and on the website). It is the part in between: what is where, what the build will refuse to let you do, and which file to open for the change you came to make.

If you are reading this to work out whether you can understand this codebase without asking anybody: that is what it is for, and so is the rest of the documentation. Every claim below is generated from the tree, so it cannot describe a repository that no longer exists.

Two programs, one engine

veilvoice is the command line and veilvoice-gui is the window. They are the only two binaries, and both are built from the same crates: the window is not a wrapper around the command line, and neither shells out to the other. What each one has that the other does not, and why, is docs/COMMANDS.md.

The verifier is folded into both rather than shipped as a third binary, so a release is checked by the program it ships beside. crates/veilvoice-verify/src/lib.rs says what that cost and why it was worth it.

Where to start, by what you came to change

Change what the veiling does to a voice

crates/veilvoice-core/src/chain.rs

The engine. Deidentifier::process is the whole of it: one block in, one block out, no allocation and no locking. Read the module comment before changing a number in it, because several of them are load bearing for the claim that the result cannot be inverted.

Add or change a command

crates/veilvoice-cli/src/main.rs

The Command enum is clap's tree and the program's own list in one place. A new variant needs a module beside it, a section in docs/COMMANDS.md through tools/docs/commands.py, and nothing else: two tests will tell you the rest.

Add or change a tab in the window

crates/veilvoice-gui/src/app.rs

enum Tab and Tab::ALL decide what the strip shows, and Tab::key names the screenshot and the anchor. Everything that counts the tabs, photographs them or documents them reads those three, so adding one is one edit and a capture run.

Change what a recording is sealed with

crates/veilvoice-crypto/src/container.rs, crates/veilvoice-crypto/src/hybrid.rs

The container format and the X25519 plus ML-KEM combiner. Any change here changes files people already have, so the format carries a version and the readers accept the old one.

Change the app lock

crates/veilvoice-crypto/src/lock.rs, crates/veilvoice-gui/src/security.rs

The stored verifier and the rate limit are in the first; the screen and the session passphrase are in the second. Both carry the same paragraph about what the lock is worth, and it is printed to the user rather than only written here.

Change the Studio, the vault or a take

crates/veilvoice-gui/src/studio.rs, crates/veilvoice-gui/src/vault_store.rs

Veiling and recording are one session with two halves; the vault is sealed with both passphrases and opens with neither alone.

Change what the monitor can see

crates/veilvoice-watch/src/lib.rs

Six observers behind one interface, each of which says what it cannot see on the platform it is running on. An empty list from a blind observer is never presented as good news, and that rule is the reason this crate exists rather than a function.

Change the website or the documentation

docs/WEBSITE.md, tools/verify.py

Nothing in website/ or docs/files/ is written by hand. The first says which script owns which page; the second runs all of them in dependency order and then checks the result.

Work out why a build is red

tools/verify.py, .github/workflows/ci.yml

python tools/verify.py --quick runs everything except the three cargo steps, which is where nearly all the surprises are: a generated file left behind by a commit that added a source file.

The rules, and why they are rules

The long version is docs/CONTRIBUTING.md. These are the ones that will stop a change getting in.

No unsafe, anywhere. Every crate carries #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. It is a publicly stated promise and it is load bearing: it is why a memory-safety claim about this program is checkable rather than a matter of trust. A feature that needs unsafe is a feature this project does not have, and two of them are named on the roadmap for exactly that reason.

Nothing in a realtime path allocates, locks or prints. An audio callback runs on the operating system's audio thread with a deadline of a few milliseconds. Every buffer is sized before the stream starts, and try_lock and try_push are the only forms used. A test reads the callbacks themselves and fails naming the line.

A dependency says what it is for, on the line that declares it. One sentence, at the moment the decision is made. If there is no sentence to write, that is the answer: it does not go in.

Where a fact exists twice, one copy is derived or checked. A version number comes from Cargo.toml, a line count from the tool that counts, a list of binaries from the job that publishes them. Anything that cannot be derived is checked in CI, so drift fails a build rather than being found by a reader.

A change is not finished until everything describing it has changed. The source, the doc comments, the generated documentation, the wiki, the website, the README, the guides, the roadmap, the packaging, the recorded sessions and the search index. The one exception is a record of the past: CHANGELOG.md and docs/AUDIT.md say what happened.

Every behavioural change carries a regression test. And a fix carries its write-up in docs/AUDIT.md, which is where the reasoning behind a guard is kept so that the next person does not remove it as unnecessary.

What a build enforces, and which file enforces it

Each of these is a script that fails a build and names the line. They are listed from the scripts themselves, so a guard added to tools/audit/ appears here without anybody remembering to write it down.

GuardWhat it will not let you do
tools/audit/actions.pyEvery GitHub Action a workflow runs is pinned to a commit, not to a tag
tools/audit/build_output.pyNo build output lives inside this repository except where it is expected
tools/audit/crate_tables.pyEvery crate in the workspace appears in every table that lists the crates
tools/audit/dependabot.pyEvery manifest in this tree is covered by a Dependabot entry, aimed at dev
tools/audit/dependencies.pyEvery dependency says what it is for, where it is declared
tools/audit/documented.pyEvery item on a generated page has something written under it
tools/audit/features.pyEvery feature selection a release builds is built here too
tools/audit/fixtures.pyA file the build needs is in the commit, not merely on the machine that wrote it
tools/audit/publishing.pyThe step that publishes a release says which commit it is publishing
tools/audit/randomness.pyEvery random number this project draws comes from a cryptographic source
tools/audit/reachable.pyEvery public item is named by something other than its own declaration
tools/audit/rsa_usage.pyNo crate reaching pgp may gain an RSA private-key code path
tools/audit/state_paths.pyFind state files that one part of VeilVoice writes and another reads

Every one of them was written after something got through. The reasoning is in docs/AUDIT.md under a finding number, which is worth reading before deciding a guard is unnecessary.

Running the checks

One command runs the lot, in dependency order, and then verifies its own output:

python tools/verify.py            # everything
python tools/verify.py --quick    # everything but the three cargo steps
python tools/verify.py --check    # verify, regenerate nothing

--quick is the one to run before a push that touches no Rust. The three it skips are the slowest and almost never the failures:

  • formatting: cargo fmt --all --check
  • clippy: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
  • tests: cargo test --workspace

What it regenerates, in the order it has to:

  • measured numbers: python tools/measured/generate.py
  • artwork: python assets/generate.py
  • release cards: python tools/release/card.py
  • screenshot borders: python tools/shots/crop.py
  • screenshot height: python tools/shots/fit.py
  • screenshot corners: python tools/shots/round.py
  • screenshot sizes on the pages: python tools/shots/attrs.py
  • terminal drawings: python tools/shots/terminal.py
  • documentation: python tools/docs/generate.py
  • every command, and its place in the window: python tools/docs/commands.py
  • the developer guide: python tools/docs/developers.py
  • per-program guides: python tools/docs/guides.py
  • wiki landing and documents: python tools/docs/wiki.py
  • demonstration data: python tools/site/demo.py
  • website source pages: python tools/docs/sources.py
  • the wiki on the website: python tools/site/wiki_site.py
  • section pages: python tools/site/split.py
  • roadmap page: python tools/site/roadmap.py
  • questions page: python tools/site/faq.py
  • releases page: python tools/site/releases.py
  • addresses and the sitemap: python tools/site/seo.py
  • search index: python tools/search-index/generate.py

  • every crate appears in every table that lists the crates: python tools/audit/crate_tables.py
  • no build output lives outside the one directory at the root: python tools/audit/build_output.py

  • every manifest is covered by a Dependabot entry: python tools/audit/dependabot.py

  • every feature selection a release builds is still declared: python tools/audit/features.py

  • artwork matches its generator: python assets/generate.py --check
  • the release cards match CHANGELOG.md: python tools/release/card.py --check

  • no screenshot has empty space below its content: python tools/shots/fit.py --check
  • screenshots have rounded corners: python tools/shots/round.py --check
  • every screenshot tag matches its file: python tools/shots/attrs.py --check
  • terminal drawings match their output: python tools/shots/terminal.py --check
  • recorded sessions match the programs: python tools/shots/sessions.py --check
  • documentation matches the source: python tools/docs/generate.py --check
  • per-program guides match the user guide: python tools/docs/guides.py --check
  • the wiki matches the documents, and every link in it resolves: python tools/docs/wiki.py --check
  • website source pages match their files: python tools/docs/sources.py --check
  • every command is documented, and its window location exists: python tools/docs/commands.py --check

  • search index matches the tree: python tools/search-index/generate.py --check

The comments

The comments are the documentation, literally. tools/docs/generate.py reads every //! and /// in the workspace and writes a page per crate and per file from them, into docs/files/, into the GitHub wiki and into website/reference/. A module comment is the top of a published page; a function comment is an entry on it.

So a comment removed is a page that loses a paragraph, and a comment rewritten to be shorter is a page that says less. The ratio of comment to code here is deliberately high and is not a defect to be cleaned up. Where a comment explains why a number is what it is, or why an obvious alternative was refused, it is usually recording a defect that was found the hard way and is written up in docs/AUDIT.md under a finding number.

Add to them rather than replacing them. If a comment has become wrong, the fix is to say what is true now, in the same detail, in the same commit as the change that made it wrong.
